items.title: Making every harness durable
items.summary: Developers are familiar with running coding agents locally through harnesses like Pi, Claude Code, and others. They are reliable daily drivers for generating code, but keeping agents running around the clock requires your computer to be on and awake, which led to the laptop lid memes and Mac mini demand spike. Harness workloads are moving to the cloud. Individual developers are deploying always-on coding agent workflows, projects like OpenWork and HanaAgent use open-source harnesses as the engines behind the apps, and engineers are building their own harness products. These harnesses are designed for long-lived processes that keep the session in memory, and agent tasks commonly run for minutes or hours. Locally, a harness has direct, continuous access to the workspace and session history on the same disk, so resuming interrupted work only requires a simple prompt. In the cloud, you can replicate that setup with a VM and persistent storage, but the VM doesn't automatically record which model and tool calls completed or resume interrupted turns after a crash. A failed turn or network error means lost work. Also, not every agent task executed through a harness needs a sandbox. Database queries and API calls can run securely in functions, and that also means required credentials never have to enter the sandbox.We built  and  to run durably in the cloud out of the box, and today we are introducing , which extends that durability to any harness, including , , , and . It uses the same machinery that powers  to survive crashes and function timeouts. evefxPiOpenCodeCodexClaude CodeWorkflow SDKdurable-harnessWith , you can: durable-harnessTake the example of a coding agent adding a pricing page to an existing app. The agent reads the existing page, writes a new one, opens a pull request, and waits for CI to finish before reporting back. What happens if its function times out while CI is still running? Kill the function or drop the connection in the demo below to compare how the two agents recover and which work is repeated.Without durability, the agent stops work until it is manually restarted, and completed work is repeated unnecessarily.With , a new function reads completed results from the log and resumes the turn. If the browser disconnects, the agent keeps running, and reconnecting catches up from the log.durable-harness is the newest package in our open source portfolio. It’s a set of adapters and utilities that let the harnesses you already use keep their sessions in a , the Workflow SDK’s durable backend.durable-harnessWorldIt writes each step of a turn to a durable log. Before a model call or tool call runs, it records an intent, and when the call finishes, it records the outcome. The turn itself is backstopped with a queue message, so if its function dies, the queue hands the turn to a new function that reads the log and continues where it left off.After a crash, the log says what finished, what was running, and what never started:Harnesses that keep their own session files, like Claude Code's transcript, Codex's rollout, and OpenCode's event store, have every record mirrored into the log, so a new function or Sandbox rebuilds them from it. and  are durable on their own. For the rest,  adds durability from the outside, without changing the harness.fxevedurable-harnessFor the full setup guide for each harness, check the .docsDurable agents need a log of each step, a way to resume a turn when its process dies, and a stream for whoever is watching.Workflow SDK ships all three behind one interface, a .World writes to that interface, so you can move the same agent from one World to another without changing its code:durable-harnessTwo variables move every agent using  to Postgres.durable-harnessFor more control, such as setting a namespace or recovering sessions when your server starts, create the World in code and pass it to your agent:Check the  for more details.self-hosting docs on Vercel shows the trace for every session, including each model call and tool call. Turns that resumed after a crash appear in the same trace, so you can see exactly where a turn stopped and picked back up.Agent RunsAn agent has only the tools you give it, and they run in your function. Each tool says what should happen if a crash interrupts it. A  tool, such as a lookup, can run again. A  tool, such as a refund, never runs twice: the model is told the call may have happened, so it can check before it tries again.
